Focus on schema enforcement, client-side vs server-side validation, error handling, and security (KMS, VPC, audit logs). Agreed next steps: share slides, security docs, sample schemas and schedule POC kick-off.
transcript:
00:00 Sofia Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Sofia from Redwood. We have Liam from the SE team with me, we'll run through JSON/structured output and our function calling demo. Can you do a quick intro?
00:08 Maya Thompson: Hi I'm Maya, product at SummitPay. Hi all. Evan here is our backend lead, Priya is security and Jordan is data eng, we'll mostly be listening and then ask integration questions.
00:20 Liam Chen: Great, thanks. Quick agenda: overview of JSON mode, show schema-driven guardrails, demo function calling for payments workflow, then Console/Optimize bits and observability. We'll also touch on security controls.
00:34 Sofia Patel: Quick qualification - are you currently prototyping with any LLM provider or self-hosted model?
00:40 Evan Ruiz: We've been testing with OpenAI for NLU and Anthropic for some experiments. Latency is a bit variable and we want stronger output guarantees - especially for structured responses we feed directly to downstream billing systems.
00:55 Priya Singh: Yes security is the other constraint, we need KMS integration, audit logs, and either VPC or private tenancy for PII-sensitive tasks.
01:06 Liam Chen: Understood. We'll show how JSON mode plus schema validation reduces misparsed outputs and how function calling can avoid hallucinated fields by constraining actions.
01:20 Sofia Patel: Ok jumping into the demo. I'll share my screen, show the API call first - simple POST to /v1/generate with mode=structured and schema param.
01:30 Liam Chen: Example schema: an object with keys transaction_id (string), amount (number), currency (enum), merchant_id (string), approved (boolean). We'll demo both soft validation (model returns best-effort) and strict validation where server rejects non-conforming responses.
01:48 Evan Ruiz: When you say server rejects - does that mean Redwood will return a 4xx? Or you attempt to auto-correct?
01:55 Liam Chen: Good question. There's a couple modes: validation_failure=reject will return structured error with diagnostics (we include token-level trace and model candidate snippets). validation_failure=repair will run a repair step - either through a deterministic transform or a constrained re-run with additional context. Both are configurable per route.
02:15 Maya Thompson: Can we see an example of a failed case?
02:18 Liam Chen: Sure. I'll run a prompt that commonly causes extra fields -
02:22 [screen noise]
02:28 Liam Chen: ...running... here's the response. Model attempted to return an extra 'discount_code' field which isn't in schema. With reject mode, the API returns 400 and body: {error: 'schema_mismatch', details: 'unexpected field discount_code', tokens:[...]}
02:48 Priya Singh: Is those tokens included in logs? Are they masked?
02:52 Liam Chen: We offer logging controls. By default we redact possible PII; customers can configure full transcript logging for troubleshooting. For Private/Dedicated we also support customer-managed KMS for encrypting logs.
03:10 Sofia Patel: Now function calling. We'll show the 'charge_payment' tool. The idea: instead of asking free-text for next steps, you define a tool schema that maps directly to your backend action and Redwood will call it when the model outputs the matched function call structure.
03:25 Liam Chen: Demo: prompt instructs model to call charge_payment with params {transaction_id, amount, currency, merchant_id}. We'll wire a fake webhook to show payloads in the console.
03:38 Jordan Park: How do you handle retries or idempotency? If model triggers multiple calls or the call fails mid-way?
03:45 Liam Chen: We surface an invocation id and provide built-in idempotency keys. You can configure retry policies per tool: exponential backoff, max attempts, and a dead-letter queue for failed invocations. We also log call results in Console with request/response payloads and timestamps.
04:03 Maya Thompson: Can the model be prevented from calling arbitrary tools?
04:07 Liam Chen: Yes, access controls are at the route level. Only registered tools for that API key/route are available. There's also per-route allowlists and RBAC so you can limit which service accounts can invoke which tools.
04:20 [30s pause while Liam flips windows]
04:52 Liam Chen: Ok here's the console: demo route 'summitpay-poc-charge' - you can see metrics, latency histograms, and per-token cost. There's an 'invocations' tab that shows function calls and the exact JSON payload the model requested.
05:08 Sofia Patel: On the Optimize side, we show recommendations for batching, cache prefixes, and suggestions to quantize models for cost savings given your average token distribution. You can simulate expected cost with sample workloads.
05:25 Priya Singh: For audit requirements we need immutable logs and legal hold. Do you support exports?
05:30 Liam Chen: Yes, we support log export to S3/GCS with retention policies and the Private product can be configured for on-prem archival. We also provide signed audit logs and an append-only change history for rollout events.
05:46 Evan Ruiz: Back to schema enforcement: do you let us run client-side validation too? We'd prefer to gate in our service before calling charge endpoints.
05:52 Liam Chen: Absolutely. Many customers run a lightweight client validation using the same JSON Schema bundle you provision in Console. We provide SDK helpers in Python/Node that validate before sending. Then server-side validation acts as the final guardrail.
06:07 Maya Thompson: Any examples of guardrails preventing hallucinated merchant IDs?
06:10 Liam Chen: Sure, we showed enums; you can also pass a merchant allowlist as part of context or as a tokenized dataset that the model can reference. In strict mode we compare returned merchant_id against your allowlist and reject if mismatch.
06:24 Priya Singh: How about PII - do you support tokenization or custom masking?
06:28 Liam Chen: We integrate with customer KMS/HSMs and have built-in PII redaction on logs. For structured fields flagged as PII we can optionally store only a hash or token reference. Those decisions are configurable per-tenant.
06:40 Sofia Patel: Ok we'll run a live flow: prompt -> model returns function call -> Redwood executes tool -> webhook shows result -> Console logs it.
06:47 [typing sounds]
07:00 Model (simulated): call: charge_payment params {"transaction_id":"txn_2459","amount":125.50,"currency":"USD","merchant_id":"m_789"}
07:12 Liam Chen: The console shows an invocation id inv_xxx; webhook returned success with provider_txn_id 'pay_9001'. We surface that back to the client as structured output.
07:29 Evan Ruiz: If the webhook fails with 5xx, will Redwood retry? And what are visibility guarantees so we don't double-charge?
07:35 Liam Chen: Retry with idempotency key prevents double-charge. And you can configure 'dry-run' mode for testing where the console logs invocations but doesn't forward to your endpoint.
07:46 Maya Thompson: Great. Switching gears: what's the recommended pattern for schema evolution? We will likely add fields over time.
07:53 Liam Chen: Best practice: use schema versioning in the route config and support backward-compatible optional fields. Redwood supports schema rollouts akin to canarying: you can serve v1 to 90% and v2 to 10% to observe regressions, then flip. We also surface per-schema validation error rates in Console.
08:12 Priya Singh: Are there quotas or throttles for function calls? For high-volume payment spikes are a concern.
08:18 Sofia Patel: You can set per-route throughput limits and burst windows. For Dedicated we provide reserved concurrency and SLA-backed latency. Hosted tier has rate-limits per account but we can add burst capacity.
08:28 Jordan Park: Integration question: do you provide middleware or example microservice code to accept and ack function calls?
08:33 Liam Chen: Yes, sample webhooks and SDKs with suggested ack patterns (202 accepted with processing updates). We'll share example Node/Python microservices.
08:44 Maya Thompson: On hallucination: you mentioned candidate snippets and token traces - can we replay model reasoning to debug why it invented a field?
08:50 Liam Chen: We include token-level trace and top-k candidates for the generation. It's not full 'thoughts' but you can see the neighboring tokens why model picked a given slot. We also tie this into our evals so you can create test prompts and guardrails regressions.
09:06 Sofia Patel: Wrapping up - quick recap and next steps?
09:10 Maya Thompson: This was helpful. Next we'll want the security docs and examples plus the cost estimate for a 3-week POC.
09:15 Sofia Patel: Okay I'll send slides and SOC2 the rest of today. Liam will send sample schema templates and SDK snippets. Evan to send payloads. We'll aim to kick off POC week of 12/22.
09:25 Evan Ruiz: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
09:28 Sofia Patel: Thanks all, end call.
